sections.description: Walks through the patient’s perioperative course, the pattern of thrombocytopenia after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), and the clinical cues that raised suspicion for HIT/aHIT despite common postoperative confounders.
subtopics: Perioperative timeline: preoperative UFH at transradial catheterization (2000 U), intraoperative UFH on CPB (45,000 U), postoperative LMWH prophylaxis (dalteparin POD1–4)
Expected platelet kinetics after CPB: typical 30%–50% drop with nadir POD2–3 and recovery by POD4–5 versus progressive/second drop suggesting HIT
Observed course: platelet fall from 210×10^9/L preop to 155×10^9/L POD1, then to 50×10^9/L by POD5; new neurological change (delirium) with CT-confirmed parietal infarct
Applying and adapting the 4Ts score after cardiac surgery: magnitude of fall, timing with recent heparin exposure, thrombosis, and few alternative explanations → high pretest probability
Why early onset is a red flag: anamnestic anti-PF4 response triggered by preoperative UFH exposure enabling HIT/aHIT before POD5

sections.section_title: Mechanisms: classic HIT versus autoimmune HIT (aHIT)
sections.description: Provides the immunopathology required to understand this case, emphasizing how aHIT differs from classic HIT and how those differences predict severity, laboratory signatures, and clinical behavior.
subtopics: PF4 biology and immune complex formation: PF4 tetramers binding polyanions (heparin, endogenous glycosaminoglycans) and formation of IgG anti-PF4 complexes
Classic HIT pathway: FcγRIIa clustering on platelets, platelet activation and serotonin release, monocyte tissue factor expression, procoagulant state with high thrombotic risk

Defining aHIT: heparin-independent platelet activation due to antibodies recognizing PF4 alone or PF4 bound to endogenous polyanions; clinical phenotypes (delayed-onset, refractory, spontaneous-like syndromes)

Why thrombosis and consumptive coagulopathy can be profound in aHIT: sustained immune activation despite heparin cessation; laboratory correlates include falling fibrinogen, rising D-dimer, and schistocytes

Interpretation of partial resistance to FcγRIIa blockade (IV.3): unusually strong/avid antibody–PF4 immune complexes and potential auxiliary pathways of activation; implications for in vitro testing and clinical severity

sections.description: Explains how alternative causes were excluded and how immunoassay and functional testing were synthesized—despite initially ‘indeterminate’ reporting—to reach a diagnosis of aHIT.
subtopics: Baseline labs and smear: isolated thrombocytopenia, stable hemoglobin, normal WBC, no early schistocytosis; early postoperative fibrinogen elevation (acute phase) with subsequent decline signaling consumptive process
Neuroimaging: cortical infarct supporting HIT-associated arterial thrombosis
PF4/polyanion ELISA: strong-positive (OD 2.2) increases likelihood of clinically significant antibodies in a high pretest probability context
Serotonin-release assay (SRA) patterns: strong activation at 0.1–0.3 U/mL heparin with inhibition at 100 U/mL (compatible with HIT); crucial aHIT clue—strong activation at 0 U/mL heparin

Atypical SRA feature: only partial inhibition by FcγRIIa-blocking mAb IV.3; why this led to an ‘indeterminate’ label and how direct review with the reference lab reclassified findings as consistent with severe aHIT

Differential diagnosis after cardiac surgery: excluding sepsis/DIC without source, CPB-related thrombocytopenia (timing and trajectory mismatch), post-transfusion purpura (no transfusion), drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia (timing), and TTP (labs/clinical picture)
Synthesis: early onset explained by preoperative UFH; thrombosis present; ELISA strongly positive; SRA shows heparin-independent activation → aHIT most probable

sections.section_title: Therapeutic strategy and monitoring in severe aHIT
sections.description: Details the stepwise treatment decisions, rationales for drug selection and adjustments, adjunctive immunotherapy, and laboratory/clinical metrics used to track control of hypercoagulability.
subtopics: Immediate steps: stop all heparins (UFH/LMWH), avoid platelet transfusions unless life-threatening bleeding, begin non-heparin anticoagulation
Initial non-heparin anticoagulant selection: argatroban (short half-life, titratable in setting of acute stroke and severe thrombocytopenia); aPTT target and hepatic considerations

Role of high-dose IVIG in aHIT: dosing (e.g., 100 g daily ×2–3), mechanism (Fc receptor saturation), and typical brisk platelet response; interpreting this patient’s attenuated response as a marker of severity

Monitoring disease activity and treatment adequacy: serial platelets plus fibrinogen and D-dimer as surrogates for consumptive coagulopathy; recognizing inadequate control (falling fibrinogen, rising D-dimer, new schistocytes)

Rationale for switching to fondaparinux: ease of use, suspected suboptimal control on argatroban; importance of antithrombin sufficiency for fondaparinux activity and indication for AT concentrate supplementation
Transition to long-term anticoagulation: criteria for switching (platelet recovery), resumption of apixaban for atrial fibrillation; typical duration of anticoagulation in HIT with thrombosis
Stroke-specific considerations: balancing ischemic and hemorrhagic risks while maintaining therapeutic anticoagulation in HIT

Documentation and future precautions: labeling heparin allergy, strategies for future procedures (consider non-heparin anticoagulants for CPB or preoperative desensitizing strategies in exceptional circumstances)

sections.section_title: Outcomes, antibody evolution, and clinical lessons
sections.description: Summarizes recovery, highlights how the serologic phenotype evolved over time, and distills practical pearls and pitfalls applicable to cardiac surgery patients with early thrombocytopenia.
subtopics: Clinical outcome: gradual platelet recovery (to 155×10^9/L by POD62; 202×10^9/L by POD87) and full neurological recovery
Antibody trajectory: persistent SRA positivity for months with evolution from heparin-independent activation to predominantly heparin-dependent reactivity (waning aHIT features)

Key diagnostic pearls: early-onset thrombocytopenia after cardiac surgery warrants scrutiny for preoperative heparin exposure; strong ELISA plus SRA activation at 0 U/mL heparin points to aHIT; engage the reference lab when SRA is reported ‘indeterminate’

Management lessons: escalate promptly if hypercoagulability markers worsen; consider fondaparinux with AT supplementation in severe/refractory aHIT; use IVIG early while recognizing that blunted response signals more severe disease

Algorithmic approach: structured evaluation of post-CPB thrombocytopenia (timeline, 4Ts in context, exclude common mimics, order ELISA and functional testing, start non-heparin anticoagulation when probability is intermediate–high)
Implications for future care: caution with re-exposure to heparin; consider antibody testing if re-exposure is unavoidable; educate the patient and care teams
